faq.q1: How much does a 1% advisory fee cost over 30 years?
faq.a1: The arithmetic shows that even a 1% annual fee can compound into a large dollar amount over long horizons. For example, on a $500,000 portfolio growing at 7% for 30 years, a 1% advisory fee reduces the ending value from about $3.8 million to roughly $2.9 million, a difference of approximately $939,000. The Cost of a Financial Advisor calculator on The Long Math lets you model this under your own assumptions.
faq.q2: Should extra money go toward paying down a mortgage or investing?
faq.a2: This site models the trade-off as a cash-flow-neutral comparison: the same monthly amount is either directed toward faster mortgage payoff or invested. The Pay Off Mortgage vs Invest calculator shows how interest rates, expected returns, and time horizon interact so you can see the arithmetic behind each scenario.
faq.q3: How does inflation change the long-term value of money?
faq.a3: Inflation compounds over time and changes the real buying power of nominal dollar amounts. The Inflation Time Machine tool converts amounts between years using historical CPI data, while the Inflation article explains how nominal and real values diverge over long horizons.
faq.q4: When do different Canadian accounts (TFSA, RRSP, FHSA) produce different outcomes?
faq.a4: Different registered accounts apply tax rules at different stages: contribution, growth, and withdrawal. The TFSA vs RRSP vs FHSA calculator models these rules explicitly so you can see how tax rates, eligibility, and time horizon change the arithmetic of each account under specific scenarios.
